title: Questions for people using AI trading tools and bots
author: Horror_Office_5737
selftext:
Hi everyone,  
I’m the founder of a small startup building a market intelligence tool. Rather than placing trades or telling people what to buy, our goal is to translate complex market data into plain English so people can understand what’s happening without spending hours analysing charts.  
We’re trying to build something that’s calm, educational and genuinely useful, and before we continue building I’d really like to hear from people who actively use AI trading tools or automated trading bots.  
A few questions:  
What do you enjoy most about using AI trading tools?  
Do you ever worry about giving an AI control over your money, or has that trust come naturally over time?  
How closely do you monitor it once it’s running?  
If you could improve one thing about the tools you currently use, what would it be?  
Is there anything you feel the market is missing that would genuinely make your day-to-day life easier?  
If you were to move away from AI trading bots in the future, what would need to exist for you to feel comfortable making your own trading decisions again?  
We’ve been building our platform for around five months, and one thing we’ve learned is that the best ideas usually come from users rather than ourselves.  
I’m not here to promote anything—I genuinely want to understand how people feel about AI trading, trading tools in general, and where you think the industry could improve.  
I’d really appreciate any thoughts or experiences you’re willing to share.

comments.author: Interesting_Gold_792
comments.body:
I've been building and paper-testing an AI trading system too, and one thing I've realized is that most products compete on signal quality when I think trust is the bigger problem.

Personally, I don't want AI to tell me "BUY" or "SELL." I want it to explain why its confidence changed, what evidence supports the idea, and—most importantly—what would make it change its mind.

If an AI can clearly explain why it's bullish today and what would invalidate that thesis tomorrow, I think users will trust it much more than another system claiming a higher win rate.

Curious if you've heard similar feedback from other builders or users.

replies.author: Horror_Office_5737
replies.body:
I actually agree with that. One of the biggest things we’ve learned while building [FlowPulse](https://theflowpulseapp.com)is that trust is far more valuable than simply producing another “buy” or “sell” signal.  
We intentionally moved away from anything that could be interpreted as telling users what to do. Instead, we’re focused on explaining *why* the market looks the way it does in plain English, leaving the decision entirely with the user.  
During our research we analysed around 70 existing platforms, and one thing that stood out was how few of them prioritised explanation over prediction. That reinforced the direction we’re taking.  
I really like your point about showing what would invalidate an AI’s thesis. I think being transparent about changing confidence is much more useful than claiming a high win rate.

So many projects are failing this year or cutting their loses. Crypto has became very fragile not only due to lack of information but rug pulls etc.  hopefully we will see crypto return to the state it once was.

replies.author: Interesting_Gold_792
replies.body:
I think there's another layer that most platforms still miss.

Explaining why the market looks bullish is valuable, but explaining why the AI decided to take (or skip) a trade is even more useful.

For me, every thesis should include two things:

• Why I currently believe this.  
• What specific evidence would make me change my mind.

That second part builds trust because users know the system has a predefined way to admit it's wrong instead of simply changing its opinion after the fact.

In my opinion, confidence isn't just a number—it's something users should be able to audit over time.

replies.author: Horror_Office_5737
replies.body:
I really like that perspective. I think that’s where a lot of trust is either built or lost.  
One thing we’ve tried to stay away from is simply telling users what to do. Our focus has been explaining what’s happening in the market and why, then letting the user make the final decision.  
I do like your idea of showing what would invalidate a thesis, though. Having a predefined reason for confidence to increase or decrease makes the reasoning much more transparent instead of feeling like the AI is just changing its mind after the fact.  
That’s definitely something I’ll be thinking about as we continue building.
